newsitem.title: CHINA: Call for change in China insurance investment rule.
newsitem.headline: Call for change in China insurance investment rule.

text.p: China should relax the current ban on insurance companies investing in shares to help stabilise the country's immature stock markets, analysts and insurance company officials said on Thursday.

Invested insurance premiums, one of the key sources of funds for the world's main stock markets, make up probably less than one percent of trading on China's markets, with much of that amount unauthorised, analysts said.
But the government has so far stopped the insurance companies from plowing their premiums into the stock markets out of fear that they might lose the funds in unwise trading, they said.

"There must eventually be some changes to the rules governing the use of capital, otherwise it is going to have an effect on the country's economy," said Feng Jialiang, a senior executive with China Pacific Insurance, one of China's main state-owned insurance firms.
"I think the central bank will gradually relax the rules, but I don't now how fast," Feng said in an interview.

A broker with a foreign insurance company in Beijing said there were stiff rules on how Chinese insurance companies could invest the premiums they take in, requiring them to place most of the money in treasury bonds and bank deposits.
"This is a major issue," the broker said. "Insurance companies would love to see it opened up more, and it would clearly be a boost for the stock markets."
He said he sensed no fundamental opposition to the idea from senior officials in the Chinese regulatory bodies such as the People's Bank of China.
"I think the benefits (of insurance premium investment in shares) has been recognised, but they need to get the regulatory framework right first," he said.
Stock brokers also are eager to see a relaxation of the rules.

"It will provide tremendous stability for the markets, because insurance companies buy blocks of blue chips and then sit on them for years," said a broker with one foreign firm in Shanghai. "Ultimately, it's the only way you're going to get volatility down."
A foreign banker said that while the rules on investment were strict, Chinese insurance companies still found ways to move funds into and out of the stock markets to at least a limited degree.
"On paper, they are not allowed to invest in speculative things, but this is China," the banker said.
He said that there was a risk in the short term that Chinese insurance companies could contribute to speculative instability on the stock markets if they took the wrong approach.
"If the insurance companies took the same short-minded, unsophisticated investment approach as other Chinese investors, it could trigger off an even more speculative market," he said.
But China Pacific's Feng said this would not happen -- insurance companies have too much at stake.
"If there was a policy change it would be good for our business, but our prestige is our life," he said. "If we lost capital in the stock market it would be disastrous."
China's insurance industry is still relatively undeveloped, but it is expanding fast.
Official figures indicate China's insurance industry took in 72.5 billion yuan in premiums in 1995, 10.5 percent more than 1994. The official forecast for premium income by 2000 is 120 billion yuan.
China Pacific's Feng said his company was expecting a 40 percent growth in business in 1996 over 1995.
($1 = 8.3 Chinese yuan)
